content.title: Acute Appendicitis

redFlags: Generalized peritonitis, rigid abdomen or rapidly worsening pain
Hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, rising lactate or other features of sepsis/shock
Imaging evidence of perforation, free air, abscess, phlegmon or diffuse contamination
Persistent or progressive right iliac fossa pain despite initially normal or equivocal tests
Pregnancy possibility, age 65 years or older, immunocompromise or severe obesity requiring population-specific assessment
symptoms: Acute abdominal pain, often beginning centrally and localizing to the right lower quadrant
Anorexia, nausea or vomiting
Pain aggravated by movement, coughing or walking
Fever or constitutional upset, which may be absent early
Atypical pain location or muted symptoms in older adults and immunocompromised patients
physicalSigns: Right lower quadrant tenderness with localized guarding or percussion/cough tenderness
Rebound or involuntary rigidity when peritoneal irritation is present
Fever, tachycardia, dehydration or reduced perfusion when systemic illness develops
A mass or prolonged symptom history suggesting phlegmon or abscess
No single symptom or sign confirms or excludes appendicitis; serial examination and structured risk assessment are required

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pregnancy possibility, pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, syncope or haemodynamic instability; obtain urgent pregnancy testing and gynaecology assessment.

differentials.condition: Ovarian torsion or ruptured ovarian cyst
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain, adnexal tenderness or mass; pelvic ultrasonography and urgent gynaecology review may be required.
Colicky flank-to-groin pain, haematuria and urinary tract imaging findings; pyuria or haematuria alone does not exclude appendicitis.
Dysuria, frequency, flank tenderness and supportive urine culture; mild urinary abnormalities can occur with appendicitis.
Diarrhoea, diffuse cramps or enteric exposure may predominate; persistent focal peritonism or progressive inflammatory markers require reassessment.
CT may show diverticular or colonic pathology; consider particularly in older adults or after a periappendiceal abscess.
Recurrent symptoms, diarrhoea, weight loss, perianal disease or ileocolonic imaging findings.
Often follows viral illness and may show enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix on imaging.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: A visualized inflamed, non-compressible appendix or supportive secondary signs increases diagnostic probability; abscess or free fluid may indicate complicated disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Use promptly when imaging is indicated and expertise is available. It can reduce CT use. A nonvisualized appendix is nondiagnostic, and accuracy is limited by operator skill, body habitus and appendix position.

Limitations include radiation, contrast risk and false-negative early disease; use pregnancy-specific imaging instead when relevant.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Persistent appendicitis or an alternative diagnosis
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Use active observation for stable intermediate-risk patients. Do not use observation to delay surgery in peritonitis, sepsis or clinical deterioration. Cross-sectional imaging is recommended before surgery for non-resolving pain with initially normal investigations.

medicationPlan.note: UNREVIEWED GOVERNED DRAFT — NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. The exact regimen above is limited to uncomplicated appendectomy prophylaxis. It is not a nonoperative or complicated-appendicitis treatment regimen. Complicated-infection drug selection and duration require the current Saudi hospital antimicrobial policy, antibiogram and stewardship review. The 2025 WSES versus 2022 Saudi MOH duration difference remains an explicit review item.

regimens.dose: Cefazolin 2 g (3 g if body weight is 120 kg or more) plus metronidazole 500 mg
regimens.duration: Single dose; total prophylaxis must not continue beyond 24 hours after surgery end time
regimens.frequency: Single preoperative dose; administer within 60 minutes before incision
regimens.indication: Surgical prophylaxis for uncomplicated appendicitis undergoing appendectomy
monitoring: Verify antibiotic administration time before incision and document weight-based cefazolin selection.
Monitor for immediate hypersensitivity during and after administration.
Check renal and hepatic function when repeated treatment, severe organ dysfunction or complicated infection is present.
If therapy continues for complicated infection, review cultures, clinical response, local antibiogram and adverse effects daily.
adjustments: Do not give cefazolin after immediate hypersensitivity to cefazolin, cephalosporins, penicillins or other beta-lactams; use the Saudi MOH alternative pathway and verify it against the local formulary.

Cefazolin repeated dosing requires renal adjustment below creatinine clearance 55 mL/min; the Saudi single-dose appendectomy table does not specify a reduced renal dose, so consult pharmacy if redosing or treatment is required.

Metronidazole is contraindicated with nitroimidazole hypersensitivity, Cockayne syndrome, or disulfiram use within 2 weeks; avoid alcohol or propylene glycol during and for at least 3 days after treatment.
Reduce metronidazole by 50% in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C); monitor for adverse effects in severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease and account for haemodialysis removal.
Pregnancy is outside this draft's governed population; use the pregnancy-specific surgical and pharmacy pathway.
regimens.patientGroup: Nonpregnant adults; confirm local formulary, allergy history and renal/hepatic status

monitoring: Renal and hepatic function when repeat treatment or severe organ dysfunction is present
Cultures and daily response if treatment continues for complicated infection
adjustments: Use cefazolin 3 g when body weight is 120 kg or more.
Repeated cefazolin dosing requires renal adjustment below creatinine clearance 55 mL/min; seek pharmacy advice because the single-dose MOH table does not specify a reduced prophylactic dose.
Reduce metronidazole by 50% in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C); monitor severe renal impairment or ESRD and account for haemodialysis removal.
Pregnancy is outside this draft's scope; use population-specific surgical and pharmacy review.

contraindications: Immediate hypersensitivity to cefazolin, cephalosporins, penicillins or other beta-lactams

pathophysiology.summary: Acute appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix. Luminal obstruction can initiate distension, bacterial overgrowth, impaired venous and lymphatic drainage, ischaemia and, in some patients, gangrene or perforation; obstruction is not demonstrated in every case. Disease is classified as uncomplicated or complicated because abscess, phlegmon, perforation or peritonitis changes the urgency, source-control plan and antibiotic duration.

keyMechanisms: Appendiceal luminal obstruction or primary mucosal inflammation increases intraluminal pressure and wall oedema.
Impaired venous and lymphatic drainage can progress to mural ischaemia and bacterial translocation.
Gangrene or perforation can produce localized abscess or phlegmon, diffuse peritonitis and sepsis.
Uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis may not represent a single inevitable linear progression, so severity must be assessed clinically and with imaging or operative findings.

content.clinicalScenario: Nonpregnant adults with suspected or confirmed acute appendicitis in Saudi emergency and inpatient care. Paediatric, pregnant, immunocompromised and frail older patients require population-specific surgical, radiology and pharmacy review before this draft is used.

clinicalManagement.title: Identify instability and complicated disease
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, observations, perfusion, hydration and abdominal signs; obtain IV access and resuscitate when indicated.
Keep the patient fasting while surgery remains possible; provide analgesia, antiemetic treatment and isotonic fluid according to clinical need and local prescribing policy.
Escalate immediately to senior emergency and surgical teams for generalized peritonitis, sepsis, shock or suspected perforation; diagnostics must not delay resuscitation or source-control planning.
Begin resuscitation and local sepsis care.
Obtain urgent surgical source-control decision and administer infection treatment under the Saudi MOH intra-abdominal infection protocol when applicable.
Proceed to structured risk stratification, laboratory testing and selective imaging.

clinicalManagement.title: Stratify probability and obtain decision-changing tests
actions: Use AIR or Adult Appendicitis Score as a decision aid, not as a stand-alone positive diagnosis.
Use active observation and timely imaging for intermediate-risk patients; use ultrasound first when appropriate and expertise is available.
Use contrast-enhanced CT when ultrasound or assessment remains equivocal and the result will change management; select a pregnancy-specific pathway if pregnancy is possible.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm severity and agree the treatment branch
actions: Obtain general surgical review and classify uncomplicated versus complicated appendicitis using clinical, imaging and operative findings.
Document patient population, appendicolith, abscess or phlegmon, perforation, comorbidity, anaesthetic risk and local resource constraints.
Use shared decision-making when operative and nonoperative options are both reasonable, including failure, recurrence and missed-complication risk.
Plan laparoscopic appendectomy on the next available operating list and within 24 hours of admission, minimizing delay.
Give the verified Saudi MOH single-dose pre-incision prophylaxis regimen unless contraindicated or replaced by the local formulary pathway.
Offer only with surgical oversight, reliable clinical monitoring, shared decision-making and rapid access to reassessment.
Select the antibiotic regimen from the current local antimicrobial policy; this draft does not infer a universal nonoperative regimen.
branches.condition: Selected uncomplicated appendicitis and antibiotic-first care considered

actions: Prioritize early source control; select laparoscopic surgery or abscess/phlegmon management according to anatomy, physiologic state and local expertise.
Use Saudi MOH intra-abdominal infection treatment categories and the current hospital antibiogram with antimicrobial stewardship review.

clinicalManagement.title: Use perioperative antibiotics by disease class
actions: For uncomplicated appendectomy, give one broad-spectrum preoperative dose within the specified pre-incision window; do not continue postoperative antibiotics when uncomplicated disease is confirmed.
For complicated disease, record adequacy of source control and review cultures, physiology and local resistance data before choosing or narrowing treatment.

Do not silently merge duration recommendations: the current WSES abstract reports 2-3 postoperative days for complicated disease, while the 2022 Saudi MOH protocol states 4 days after adequate source control. A Saudi antimicrobial stewardship and surgical reviewer must select the local rule before approval.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before incision and after source control

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge, pathology and follow-up
actions: Confirm stable observations, oral intake, pain control, mobility, wound plan and absence of an untreated complication before discharge.
Send appendectomy specimens for histopathology and review the result through the responsible surgical service.

After nonoperative treatment, provide explicit deterioration and recurrence instructions and arrange surgical follow-up; after a periappendiceal abscess, use an age- and risk-appropriate neoplasm detection strategy selected by the surgical team.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before discharge and at the documented follow-up interval

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Surgical follow-up must review recovery, wound concerns and histopathology after appendectomy. Nonoperative care requires a named follow-up interval and rapid-access failure plan. After complicated appendicitis with periappendiceal abscess, the surgical team must document an age- and risk-appropriate strategy to detect appendiceal or colorectal neoplasm; the exact 2025 recommendation should be checked in the full guideline during clinical review.
mdtReferrals: General surgery for all confirmed or strongly suspected appendicitis
Radiology for staged ultrasound, CT, MRI or image-guided abscess drainage
Antimicrobial stewardship or infectious diseases for complicated infection, resistant-organism risk or unresolved duration choice
Obstetrics and gynaecology for pregnancy or gynaecologic differential diagnoses
Anaesthesia and critical care for physiologic instability or high perioperative risk
lifestyleAndDiet: Remain fasting while surgery or urgent source control is being considered; resume diet according to the treating surgical team's postoperative plan.
After discharge, increase activity gradually and follow the surgical team's wound, lifting and return-to-work advice.
Do not impose long-term dietary restriction solely because of appendicitis.
patientEducation: Explain the working diagnosis, whether disease appears uncomplicated or complicated, and why observation, imaging, surgery or selected antibiotic-first care is being proposed.
Use shared decision-making for nonoperative care and explain early failure, later recurrence and the need for immediate reassessment if symptoms worsen.
Give written wound, medicine and red-flag instructions in the patient's preferred language before discharge.
dischargeCriteria: Stable observations without untreated sepsis, peritonitis or evolving complication
Pain and nausea controlled on an agreed outpatient plan
Tolerating oral intake and mobilising safely when required by the treatment pathway
Operation, pathology and antibiotic plans documented with responsible follow-up service
Patient understands recurrence or deterioration red flags and has reliable access to urgent reassessment
